name: LPC1768FBD100K
title: LPC176x Cortex-M3 microcontrollers: 512 kB flash, 64 kB SRAM, Ethernet, USB OTG, CAN (LPC1769/68/67/66/65/64/63)
summary: The LPC176x is a family of Cortex-M3 microcontrollers running at up to 100 MHz (120 MHz for LPC1769) from a single 2.4 V to 3.6 V supply, with up to 512 kB flash and 64 kB SRAM. Depending on the part it carries a 10/100 Ethernet MAC, full-speed USB device/host/OTG, two CAN channels, I2S and a 10-bit DAC; every part has four UARTs, SPI, two SSPs, three I2C, an 8-input 12-bit ADC, eight-channel DMA, timers, PWM, motor control PWM, a quadrature encoder interface and a battery-backed RTC. Up to 70 GPIO come out in LQFP100, TFBGA100 or WLCSP100.
key_figures: 42 mA typ at 100 MHz, 7 mA at 12 MHz

operation.text: LPC1769, LPC1768, LPC1767, LPC1766, LPC1765, LPC1764 and LPC1763 share one Cortex-M3 design in 100-pin packages and differ in flash, SRAM, Ethernet, USB, CAN, I2S, DAC and top clock. LPC1769 runs to 120 MHz, the rest to 100 MHz. All are pin-compatible with the 100-pin ARM7 LPC236x series. Every part number carries a unique serial number.

ARM Cortex-M3: Thumb-2, hardware divide, three-stage pipeline (fetch, decode, execute overlap), Harvard buses for instructions (I-code) and data (D-code) plus a system bus, a prefetch unit with speculative branching, and an integrated NVIC with wake-up controller. A memory protection unit splits memory into up to 8 regions of 8 subregions each; an access outside the allowed regions raises a Memory Management Fault.

Up to 512 kB flash behind a two-port accelerator that allows zero-wait-state running at 120 MHz; programmed in system (ISP) or by the application (IAP) through the boot ROM. SRAM is 64 kB: 32 kB on the CPU's local bus plus two 16 kB AHB blocks (LPC1764: 16 kB local plus one 16 kB AHB block, 32 kB in all) usable by Ethernet, USB and DMA, all three reachable at once. The AHB peripheral space is 2 MB (128 slots) and the APB space 1 MB (64 slots), each peripheral getting 16 kB. A multilayer AHB matrix gives each bus master (CPU, GPDMA, Ethernet, USB) its own path; APB is split in two to cut CPU/DMA contention.

NVIC with 33 vectored interrupts, 32 priority levels with masking, relocatable vector table, NMI and software interrupts. The vector table may sit anywhere in the lowest 1 GB, aligned to 128 words (512 bytes). Any of the 42 pins of ports 0 and 2 can interrupt on rising, falling or both edges whatever function it has; this detection is asynchronous and works with clocks stopped, so each can wake the chip from power-down. EINT0 to EINT3 add up to four level- or edge-sensitive interrupt inputs.

Each pin's function is chosen by multiplexer registers. Assign the pin before enabling the peripheral and its interrupts; a peripheral running without a pin mapped behaves undefined. Most pins can also be set open-drain, and can have their pull-up, their pull-down, or neither switched on. All I/O comes out of reset as inputs; standard I/O defaults to input with pull-up.

A standard I/O pin with analog function offers: output driver with or without open-drain; input with pull-up, pull-down or repeater mode, each on or off; analog input. The pull-up and pull-down are weak MOS devices that behave like resistors.

Eight channels, 16 request lines, single and burst requests, memory and peripheral transfers in any combination, linked-list scatter/gather, a four-word FIFO per channel, 8/16/32-bit transfers, either endianness (little at reset), and interrupts on completion or error. Served peripherals: SSP0/1, all UARTs, I2S, ADC, DAC, and two match signals per timer.

Up to 70 GPIO (100-pin package) on the AHB for fast access: set/clear registers, mask registers, byte and half-word access, whole-port writes, bit-banding and DMA. Every GPIO can be pulled up, pulled down or made open-drain.

10/100 Mbit/s MAC (LPC1769/68/67/66/64) with its own scatter/gather DMA, RMII to an outside PHY and MIIM for PHY registers. IEEE 802.3 and 802.3x flow control, VLAN frames, receive filtering, multicast/broadcast, CRC insertion, padding, any frame length, promiscuous mode, automatic retransmission, and wake-on-LAN by receive filter or magic frame. Bus clock up to 100 MHz (120 MHz on LPC1769).

USB 2.0 full-speed device, host and OTG with on-chip PHY (LPC1769/68/66/65; device only on LPC1764). Device: 12 Mbit/s, 32 physical (16 logical) endpoints, 4 kB endpoint RAM, control/bulk/interrupt/isochronous, SoftConnect and GoodLink, DMA, wake from reduced-power modes on bus activity. Host: OHCI, one downstream port, port power switching. OTG: HNP and SRP support, needs an external transceiver (CEA-2011) driven over a dedicated master-only I2C interface.

If VDD is always up whenever VBUS is at 5 V, as in a bus-powered device, the VBUS pin can go straight to the connector. Where VDD can be 0 V with VBUS applied, the pin must be kept below 3.6 V, for example with a resistor divider whose output still exceeds 0.7 VDD for a HIGH.

Two CAN 2.0B controllers (ISO 11898-1) at up to 1 Mbit/s each (LPC1769/68/66/65/64), a global acceptance filter for 11-bit and 29-bit identifiers on all buses, and FullCAN automatic reception with interrupts.

One 12-bit successive-approximation ADC with eight multiplexed inputs, 200 kHz conversion rate, range VREFN to VREFP, single or burst conversion, conversion on a pin edge or timer match, a result register per channel, power-down and DMA. Used at 10 bits it converts faster.
10-bit resistor-string DAC (LPC1769/68/67/66/65/63) with buffered output, selectable drive, its own conversion timer, power-down and DMA. Full scale is VREFP.

Four UARTs with 16550-compatible registers, 16-byte FIFOs (receive trigger at 1, 4, 8 or 14 bytes), fractional baud generator, auto-baud and DMA; top rate 6.25 Mbit/s. The fractional generator reaches standard rates such as 115200 Bd from any crystal above 2 MHz. UART1 adds modem lines, auto-CTS/RTS and RS-485/9-bit with software or automatic address detection; UART3 adds IrDA.
One SPI master/slave, full duplex, 8 to 16 bits per transfer, at most 12.5 Mbit/s and at most one eighth of its input clock.

Two SSP controllers for SPI, 4-wire TI SSI or Microwire, master or slave, 4- to 16-bit frames, 8-frame transmit and receive FIFOs and DMA. Top speed 33 Mbit/s as master and 8 Mbit/s as slave; as slave the SSP clock must not exceed PCLK/12.

Three I2C controllers, each master, slave or both, multi-master with arbitration and clock synchronisation, several slave addresses and a monitor mode for watching the bus. I2C0 has true open-drain pins and reaches Fast-mode Plus, 1 Mbit/s; I2C1 and I2C2 sit on standard I/O pins and reach 400 kbit/s.

I2S with separate transmit and receive channels, each master or slave; 8/16/32-bit words, mono or stereo, 16 kHz to 96 kHz (16, 22.05, 32, 44.1, 48, 96 kHz), master clock in or out, settable word-select period, two 8-word FIFOs with level interrupts and two DMA requests, and separate reset, stop and mute for input and output.

Four 32-bit timer/counters with 32-bit prescalers, each with two capture inputs and four match registers (interrupt, stop or reset on match) driving up to four outputs (set, clear, toggle or nothing). Two match registers per timer can raise DMA requests. Eight capture inputs and ten match outputs in all.

PWM1 is a timer with seven match registers: MR0 sets the period, and the others give up to six single-edge or three double-edge outputs, or a mix. Single-edge outputs all rise at the start of the cycle; double-edge outputs place both edges anywhere, so pulses can be positive or negative. New match values take effect only when released by software, in step with the cycle, so no glitch pulses appear. Without PWM mode it is a plain 32-bit timer.

The motor control PWM drives three-phase motors, with feedback inputs (MCI0 to MCI2) and an abort input (MCABORT) that releases all drive outputs at once. The quadrature encoder interface counts position (x2 or x4), direction, velocity with a built-in timer and a less-than compare, index revolutions, with three position compares, an index compare, input filtering and clock/direction input mode.

The RI timer is a 32-bit counter on PCLK compared with a masked 32-bit value, interrupting on a match and optionally clearing itself. The Cortex-M3 SysTick, meant for a 10 ms tick, runs from the AHB clock or from the STCLK pin.

Once enabled by software the watchdog can only be turned off by a hardware or watchdog reset. A missed or wrong feed sequence gives a reset or interrupt. Its clock is the IRC, the RTC oscillator or the APB clock, so it can run free of the crystal. It has a 32-bit counter with prescaler, a reset flag, a debug mode and a lock feature.

The RTC draws under 1 µA and keeps time, calendar (seconds to year, day of week and of year) and an alarm that wakes the chip from any reduced-power mode with 1 s resolution. It runs from VDD(REG)(3V3) while present, so the battery is only drained when that supply is gone; on battery it keeps working down to 2.1 V, and a 3 V lithium cell suits it. A 32 kHz oscillator gives the 1 Hz count clock; calibration holds error under 1 s per day at fixed voltage and temperature. 20 bytes of backup registers live on VBAT.

Three oscillators: the main oscillator (1 MHz to 25 MHz crystal), the 4 MHz IRC (trimmed to 1 % over voltage and temperature) and the 32 kHz RTC oscillator. Any of them can feed PLL0 and the CPU. After power-up or any reset the chip runs from the IRC until software switches, so it starts without a crystal and the boot loader knows its frequency. Each peripheral has its own clock divider (PCLK). CLKOUT can show CCLK, the IRC, the main oscillator, the RTC clock or the USB clock.

PLL0 takes 32 kHz to 25 MHz, divides by N (1 to 256), multiplies by M (1 to 32768) in a CCO that must run between 275 MHz and 550 MHz, and the result is divided down for the CPU and/or USB. It is off and bypassed after reset and in power-down; software sets it up, waits for lock and then connects it.

PLL1 runs from the main oscillator only, accepts 10 MHz to 25 MHz and gives a fixed 48 MHz with 50 % duty to the USB block alone. It is off after reset; while it stays off the USB clock comes from PLL0 at 48 MHz.

Power-up and wake from power-down both run on the IRC so the chip resumes quickly. When the main oscillator starts, the wake-up timer holds off its use until it is stable; how long that takes depends on the VDD(3V3) ramp, the crystal and the parts round it and the conditions.

Sleep stops the core clock; peripherals run and any interrupt or reset resumes. Deep-sleep stops the oscillator and all internal clocks but keeps registers and SRAM, the IRC stays powered (output off), the RTC oscillator runs, PLL is disconnected and the CCLK and USB dividers reset to zero; flash stays powered. Code resumes 4 cycles after wake if the IRC was the clock, 4096 cycles if the main oscillator was. Power-down adds turning off the IRC and the flash: the IRC needs 60 µs to start, code in SRAM resumes 4 IRC cycles later, and the flash becomes available after its 100 µs start-up counted on the IRC. Deep power-down is entered only through the RTC and leaves only the RTC and the RESET pin powered; RESET or an RTC alarm wakes it. After any wake the PLL and dividers have to be set up again.

As the CPU goes into any of the three clock-stopped modes the NVIC hands the WIC a mask of the interrupts that are enabled and of high enough priority; the WIC wakes the CPU when one of them fires, without periodic polling. Interrupts that work in power-down include the external interrupts, RTC, USB activity, Ethernet wake-up, CAN activity, port 0/2 pin interrupts and NMI.

VDD(3V3) powers the I/O pads; VDD(REG)(3V3) powers the regulator that feeds the core, memories, peripherals, oscillators and PLLs. Tying both to one 3.3 V supply is the simple choice; separate supplies let the pad ring be switched off while the CPU and peripherals keep running. VBAT feeds only the RTC domain (RTC, backup registers, 32 kHz oscillator) through a power selector. VDDA, VREFP, VREFN and VSSA form the ADC/DAC domain. Peripheral power control can stop the clock to any unused block.

Four reset sources: the RESET pin (Schmitt trigger), the watchdog, power-on reset and brownout. Any of them drives RSTOUT LOW and starts the wake-up timer, which holds reset until the external reset is gone, the oscillator runs, a fixed count of clocks has elapsed and flash initialisation is done. RSTOUT returns HIGH when reset ends (for a BOD reset, once the supply is back above the threshold). Execution then starts at address 0, which at first maps to the boot block. The RESET pin has a pull-up and a 20 ns RC glitch filter.

The BOD watches VDD(REG)(3V3) in two stages: below 2.2 V it raises an interrupt (or a status bit software can poll); below 1.85 V it holds the chip in reset so the flash is not disturbed, and keeps it there down to about 1 V where power-on reset takes over. Both thresholds have hysteresis.

CRP is set by writing a pattern to a reserved flash location; IAP is not affected. CRP1 blocks JTAG and allows partial flash update (not sector 0) with a limited ISP command set. CRP2 blocks JTAG and allows only full erase and reprogramming through a reduced ISP set. CRP3 blocks JTAG and ISP entirely, including the P2[10] ISP entry, leaving updates to the application through IAP or a reinvoked ISP over UART0; after CRP3 no factory testing is possible.
A LOW on P2[10]/EINT0/NMI during reset starts the ISP command handler.

JTAG, serial wire debug with serial wire trace output, and parallel trace (TRACECLK, TRACEDATA[3:0]); an embedded trace module gives non-intrusive instruction trace. Eight breakpoints and four watchpoints.
Single 3.3 V supply, 2.4 V to 3.6 V. In each of the four reduced-power modes an on-chip PMU retunes the internal regulators automatically for the least current.

Main oscillator unused: XTAL1 open or grounded (grounded preferred against noise), XTAL2 open. RTC unused: VBAT to VDD(REG)(3V3), RTCX1 open; when used, the RTC needs a 32 kHz crystal. ADC and DAC unused: VDDA and VREFP to 3.3 V. The analog supplies and references are kept nominally at their digital counterparts but separate from them for low noise and error.

The oscillator input is limited to 1.8 V. An outside clock is coupled to XTAL1 through 100 pF with an amplitude of 200 mV RMS to 1000 mV RMS, which for a square wave is 280 mV to 1.4 V swing; a capacitor Cg to ground can scale a larger clock down. XTAL2 can be left open.
The feedback resistor is on chip, so a fundamental-mode crystal needs only CX1 and CX2. The crystal's parallel capacitance CP should not exceed 7 pF; FOSC, CL, RS and CP come from the crystal maker.

Put the crystal as near the oscillator pins as possible. The load capacitors (CX1, CX2, and CX3 for a third-overtone crystal) and the other outside parts share one ground plane. Keep loops and parasitics small to limit coupled noise, and reduce CX1 and CX2 to make up for the board's added parasitic capacitance.
Data is written to flash in 256-byte blocks; writing 256 bytes from RAM takes about 1 ms and erasing a sector about 100 ms.
